title: Chapter 6. When there are no politicians, conflicts come to an end

blocks.text: Pedro says it in a way that leaves little room for ambiguity: “When there are no politicians, conflicts come to an end.” The sentence is his, and this chapter takes it seriously, without turning it into a shout or an attack on any person. No office-holder is named here, nor a party, nor a face. What is spoken of is a trade: that of professional politics, that class of people whose task, in the societies we have given ourselves, is to contest power, keep it and administer it, almost always on a board where money and economic power are not an ornament, but the floor.

blocks.text: The idea has a root we have already travelled. If work was priced in coins, and if money ended up measuring people and countries, it was almost inevitable that a profession should arise devoted to sharing out, promising, regulating and fighting over that sharing out. Not everyone who takes part in public life does so for profit, and it would be unjust, as well as false, to paint them all with the same brush. There are honest vocations. There are offices taken as a service. This book does not come to deny them. It comes to ask whether the conflict that tires us so much — that of trenches, of blocs, of the permanent fight over the budget, the perk, the story that wins votes — is not born, in large measure, of the struggle for money and for the power that money holds up. If that struggle were to die down, would the trade remain standing? Would the conflicts remain standing, with the same fury?

blocks.text: Pedro answers no. Without money as the axis, and without the contest for economic power, professional politics would lose its fuel. What would remain is public business, which is something else: the care of what is held in common, the decisions about the lagoon, the school, the road, energy, food, people's time. That public business does not disappear. It changes hands. It passes to the people, who vote directly, and to an artificial intelligence that helps them decide, not rule.

blocks.text: Once again, the nuance is needed. Not all disagreements are about money. Two neighbours can argue over a noise, a boundary, a custom, an idea of the sacred, the way of educating, what should be remembered and what forgotten. Those disagreements do not evaporate because a mint is shut. A society without any conflict at all would not be a society: it would be a silence, and forced silence is not peace. What this chapter holds, in Pedro's voice, is another claim, more precise: that a huge part of the conflicts that today fill the news, parliaments and networks — those that divide a country into camps, that turn every decision into a war of attrition — is threaded on the yarn of profit and of power. Cut that yarn, and those conflicts deflate. Differences remain, which can be talked through. The profession of living off that fight does not remain, or remains far less.

blocks.text: How, then, is society organised? Not from an empty palace, and not from a machine that decrees. The picture Pedro proposes is simpler, and more demanding. People inform themselves, debate and vote directly on the questions that concern them. Artificial intelligence gathers data, orders arguments, warns of consequences, translates, explains what is difficult in a language that can be understood, and does not hide what it does not know. Then it is silent. The one who decides is the person, or the body of persons. AI is not a sovereign. It is a wise clerk, an adviser who takes no commission, a map. The map does not walk for you.

blocks.text: In a district such as this, the picture can be brought down to earth. What do we do with the Mar Menor? How are water, land, tourism, fishing, the garden to be shared? Today those questions pass through offices, deadlines, interests, campaigns. Tomorrow, in the dream of this book, they could pass through a square — physical or digital — where each person sees the same figures, the same options, the same risks, and votes. Not once every four years, choosing a whole package of promises, but when the decision asks for it, on the concrete matter. Politics would cease to be a trade of permanence and would become again what it should never have ceased to be: the conversation of those affected about what is common to them.

blocks.text: For that not to be chaos, method is needed. Information must be verifiable, as has been attempted in these pages with the figures that are cited. No one, neither a company nor a government nor a machine, must have a monopoly of the facts. The vote must be of persons, not of whoever can pay for more advertisements. And, above all, the AI must be designed not to rule: with no interests of its own, with no power to close the debate, without the trick of presenting as unique an option that is not. In other books of Pedro's, that idea has appeared as human agency: intelligences collaborate, they do not subordinate. Here it is applied to public life.

blocks.text: Some will smile and say that people do not want to decide, or do not know how, or grow tired. Sometimes it is true that people are tired. They are tired, in part, because they have been left outside, and are called only to approve a camp. Whoever has not been truly invited to the table ends up taking no interest in the table. A direct democracy, helped by a clear AI, does not guarantee wisdom. It guarantees, at least, that the decision is not the property of a profession. Mistakes would still exist. They would, though, be our mistakes, not a product sold to us every campaign.

blocks.text: Some will fear, with reason, the tyranny of a majority, or of an algorithm that pretends to be neutral. That fear should stay in the room, not in the street of forgetting. A society that votes directly needs limits that are not voted on every morning: the dignity of each person, the care of the lagoon, the right not to be crushed by the number. AI can help watch over those limits if it is built for that. It cannot itself be the limit. The limit is ethical, and it is human.

blocks.text: This chapter does not ask for a vacuum of power so that the strongest may fill it. It asks the opposite: that the power to command, when it is no longer tied to money, should dissolve into shared decisions. That there should be no permanent class living off the fight. That conflicts of profit should die down with profit itself. And that the other conflicts, the real ones, should be treated by talking, voting and caring, with an intelligence that clarifies, and with a lagoon in front, so as not to forget what public business is about: what is common to us, and should not be sold.

blocks.text: When there are no professional politicians, Pedro says, conflicts come to an end. Let that be understood, as the page closes, in its most honest sense: the conflicts that were, at bottom, a business come to an end. What remains is called living together.

blocks.text: In practice, a day of that other arrangement could be more routine than it sounds. A question is published: water, a school timetable, a work, a rule for the lagoon. The AI presents, in a clear language, what is known, what is disputed, what it would cost — if cost is still spoken of — and whom it would affect. People ask. The questions are answered with sources, not with slogans. There is a vote. It is applied. It is reviewed. No one makes a career of having won. No one lives off having lost. Conflict, when it appears, appears over the matter, not over the spoils of governing.

blocks.text: It is not a calendar utopia. It is a method. And the method, in order not to be corrupted, would have to be public to the bone: open data, reproducible reasoning, an auditable AI, a right to dissent that does not go out when the count ends. Pedro believes that, then, the conflicts that today steal our patience would have come to an end. This chapter goes with him, and notes the one thing that must not be forgotten: peace does not consist in no one thinking differently. It consists in the difference not being a business.
